title: Stopping times and optional stopping proved
objectives: Prove the optional stopping theorem under bounded stopping times.

screens.title: Stopping a fair walk
screens.prose: A fair walk starts at 3 and stops the first time it hits 0 or 10. Here are 300 such walks, 30 drawn. The lower panel averages the stopped value $S_T$ over the first $k$ walks. Move the ends to see what it follows.

derive.caption: {{values.hitsUp}} of {{values.paths}} walks hit the top. Average of $S_T$: {{fixed(values.stopped, 2)}}.

screens.question: With ends 0 and 10, what does the average of $S_T$ settle near?

hints.text: Watch the dashed line in the lower panel.
It marks the start value, and the average hugs it.
Move an end: the average still follows the start.

feedback.correct: The average settles on the start, 3. Stopping did not change the mean of a fair game.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read where the lower panel flattens out.

byKey.mid: You gave the midpoint of 0 and 10. The walk is fair, so its mean stays at the start, not at the middle.
byKey.top: You gave the upper end. Only some walks reach 10, so the average sits well below it.
byKey.share: You gave the share that hit 10. The panel averages the stopped value, not the share.

explain.text: 90 of the 300 walks reached 10 and the other 210 ended at 0. Yet the average of $S_T$ settled at 3.00, the start. Stopping at the ends leaves the mean of a fair game where it was, which is what we now prove.

screens.title: Which rules are stopping times
screens.prose: A **stopping time** $T$ decides from the past alone: $\{T = n\} \in \mathcal{F}_n$ for every $n$. At step $n$ you must be able to say whether you stop now.
screens.question: Select all that apply: which are stopping times?

options.text: The first time $S$ hits 0 or 10
$T = 5$, always stop at step 5
The smaller of two stopping times
The first time $S \ge 1$ after step 3
The last visit to 3 before step 50
options.why: You used a time that needs the future. A visit is the last only once step 50 has passed.

options.text: The step of the highest point of the first 10 steps
options.why: You used the highest point. You cannot tell a step is the highest until step 10.

hints.text: At step $n$, can you tell whether $T = n$ using steps up to $n$?
Rules about the last or the highest need the whole stretch.
A first time of something is always decided as it happens.

feedback.correct: The first four are decided as they happen. A last visit and a highest point are not.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether the rule needs steps after $n$ to say $T = n$.

byKey.e: The last visit cannot be known until the time window ends.
byKey.f: The highest point needs steps up to 10, so it looks ahead.

explain.text: A first hit, a fixed time and the smaller of two stopping times are decided by steps up to $n$. The first time $S \ge 1$ after step 3 is too. The last visit and the highest point need steps still to come, so they are not.

screens.title: The stopped process is a martingale
screens.prose: Let $M$ be a martingale and $T$ a stopping time. The stopped process is $M_{T \wedge n}$. We show it is a martingale. Two lines may swap, and one line is flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order, a reason in each line. Move the flawed line to Left out.

lines.text: Let $H_k = \mathbf{1}_{\{T \ge k\}}$: hold 1 unit on step $k$ until we stop, and 0 after.
$\{T \ge k\}$ is the complement of $\{T \le k - 1\} \in \mathcal{F}_{k-1}$, so $H_k$ is predictable and bounded.
$M_{T \wedge n} = M_0 + \sum_{k \le n} H_k (M_k - M_{k-1})$: the sum counts every step up to time $T$.
That is a martingale transform of $M$ by $H$, so $M_{T \wedge n}$ is a martingale (lesson 12). $\blacksquare$
$H_k = \mathbf{1}_{\{T > k\}}$ is predictable, since it is the same as $H_k$ but easier to write.
lines.why: You used $\{T > k\}$. It is the complement of $\{T \le k\}$, decided at time $k$ and not $k - 1$, so it is not predictable.

hints.text: A position must be fixed before the step it is held over.
$H_k = 1$ exactly when you have not stopped before step $k$.
Check predictable, write the sum, then call the transform.

feedback.correct: Right. The stopped process is gains from a predictable position, so it is fair.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Define the position, check it is predictable, then identify the transform.

byKey.x1: You used a line that places the position one step too late. $\{T \ge k\}$ is the one known at time $k - 1$.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the flawed line goes to Left out.

explain.text: $H_k = 1$ until we stop and 0 after. It is known at time $k - 1$ because $T \le k - 1$ is. So $M_{T \wedge n}$ is a martingale transform, which lesson 12 showed to be a martingale.

screens.title: Optional stopping, bounded case
screens.prose: Now let $T \le N$ be a stopping time. We prove $E[M_T] = E[M_0]$ from the last screen. Two lines may swap, and two lines are flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order, a reason in each line. Move the two flawed lines to Left out.

lines.text: Since $T \le N$, we have $T \wedge N = T$, so $M_T = M_{T \wedge N}$.
$M_{T \wedge n}$ is a martingale, so $E[M_{T \wedge N}] = E[M_{T \wedge 0}] = E[M_0]$.
Hence $E[M_T] = E[M_0]$: a bounded stopping time cannot change the mean of a fair game. $\blacksquare$
So $E[M_T] = E[M_0]$ for every stopping time, bounded or not.
lines.why: You dropped the bound. Without it $M_{T \wedge n}$ need not converge to $M_T$ in mean, and the end of this lesson shows it can fail.
You replaced $T$ by $N$. The stopped value is $M_T$, which equals $M_N$ only on paths where $T = N$.

hints.text: Use the bound to turn $M_T$ into a stopped value at a fixed time.
The mean of a martingale does not move with $n$.
Order: replace $T$, use the martingale, conclude.

feedback.correct: Right. The bound makes $M_T$ a value of the stopped martingale, whose mean is fixed.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Turn $M_T$ into a stopped value at time $N$ first.

byKey.y1: You used a line that drops the hypothesis. The theorem is for bounded $T$.
byKey.y2: You used a line that replaces the stopped value by the final one.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the two flawed lines go to Left out.

explain.text: A bounded $T$ makes $M_T$ equal to the stopped value $M_{T \wedge N}$. That is a martingale evaluated at time $N$, so its mean is $E[M_0]$. The constant $N$ is what lets us stop the argument at a finite time.

screens.title: Unbounded times, and level 2
screens.prose: The exit time $T$ from $(0, 10)$ is not bounded, but it is finite almost surely and $|S_{T \wedge n}| \le 10$. Dominated convergence gives $E[S_T] = 3$, so $P(\text{hit } 10) = \tfrac{3}{10}$. Now use $S_n^2 - n$: $E[S_{T \wedge n}^2] - E[T \wedge n] = 9$.
screens.question: Let $n \to \infty$. Which theorem handles which term?

options.text: Monotone for $E[T \wedge n]$, dominated for $E[S^2_{T \wedge n}]$
Dominated convergence for both of the terms in the identity
options.why: You dominated $T \wedge n$. It has no fixed bound, and $E[T] < \infty$ is what we are finding. It increases to $T$, which is monotone convergence.

options.text: Monotone convergence for both of the terms in the identity
options.why: You applied monotone convergence to $S^2_{T \wedge n}$. It rises and falls, but it is bounded by 100, so dominated convergence applies.

options.text: Neither: both limits are obvious from the picture, so no theorem is used
options.why: You skipped the theorem. Swapping a limit and an expectation is what level 2 proves.

hints.text: One term is increasing, and the other is bounded.
$T \wedge n$ rises with $n$. $S^2_{T \wedge n}$ stays below $10^2$.
Increasing and non-negative is monotone. Bounded is dominated.

feedback.correct: $E[T \wedge n] \uparrow E[T]$ by monotone convergence, and $E[S^2_{T \wedge n}] \to E[S_T^2]$ by dominated convergence with bound 100.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Match increasing with monotone and bounded with dominated.

byKey.b: The only bound on $T \wedge n$ is $T$, and $E[T] < \infty$ is what we are finding. It increases to $T$, which is monotone convergence.
byKey.c: $S^2_{T \wedge n}$ is not increasing, so monotone convergence does not apply.

explain.text: $T \wedge n$ increases to $T$, so monotone convergence gives $E[T \wedge n] \uparrow E[T]$. $S^2_{T \wedge n} \le 100$ and converges to $S_T^2$, so dominated convergence gives $E[S_{T \wedge n}^2] \to E[S_T^2]$.

screens.title: The expected duration
screens.prose: In the limit, $S_T$ is 10 with chance $\tfrac{3}{10}$ and 0 otherwise, so $E[S_T^2] = 100 \times \tfrac{3}{10} = 30$. And $E[S_{T \wedge n}^2] - E[T \wedge n] = 9$ becomes $E[S_T^2] - E[T] = 9$.
screens.question: What is $E[T]$?

hints.text: Rearrange $E[S_T^2] - E[T] = 9$.

feedback.correct: 21 steps on average, found with no equations to solve.

byKey.thirty: You gave $E[S_T^2]$. The 9 comes off it, because $S_n^2 - n$ started at 9.
byKey.sum: You added 9. The identity says $E[S_T^2]$ is larger than $E[T]$ by 9.
byKey.nine: You gave the constant on the right. $E[T] = E[S_T^2] - 9$.

explain.text: $E[T] = E[S_T^2] - 9 = 30 - 9 = 21$. The same result comes from $k(N - k) = 3 \times 7$. The walk lasts 21 steps on average although a few walks last much longer.

screens.title: When it fails
screens.prose: Start at 0 and stop at the first hit of $+1$, with no lower end. The walk reaches $+1$ sooner or later, so $S_T = 1$ always, and $E[S_T] = 1 \ne 0 = E[S_0]$. Optional stopping fails here. The picture draws 200 steps, so a few walks are still below 1.
screens.question: Which hypothesis breaks?

options.text: No integrable variable dominates the stopped walk
$T$ is not a stopping time
options.why: You doubted the stopping time. $\{T = n\}$ is decided by the first $n$ steps, so it is one.

options.text: $S_n$ is not a martingale
options.why: You blamed the walk. It is fair, so it is a martingale; the failure is in swapping limit and mean.

options.text: $T$ is infinite with positive chance, so no mean exists
options.why: You assumed $T$ can be infinite. A fair walk hits $+1$ almost surely; the trouble is that $E[T] = \infty$.

hints.text: Which tool in the proof needs a dominating variable?
$S_{T \wedge n}$ can dip very deep before it reaches $+1$.
No integrable variable bounds all those dips.

feedback.correct: The stopped values dip without a bound, so dominated convergence does not apply.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the step in the proof that needs a dominating variable.

byKey.b: The rule is a first-hit time, which is a stopping time.
byKey.d: The walk does reach $+1$; what has infinite mean is the time and the depth of the dips.

explain.text: $T$ is finite almost surely and $S$ is a martingale, but $\sup_n |S_{T \wedge n}|$ has infinite mean. So $E[S_{T \wedge n}] = 0$ cannot be carried to $E[S_T]$. Add a floor, and the walk may stop at the floor instead; cap the time, and $E[S_{T \wedge N}] = 0$.

screens.title: Stopping at the top
screens.prose: A backtest stops each path at its highest point in the first 10 steps. The bars show the exact chances of that maximum $M$ for the fair walk from 0. A colleague says the walk is fair, so $E[S_T]$ is 0.
screens.question: What is $E[S_T]$ when $T$ is the step of the maximum?

hints.text: At the highest point, $S_T$ is the maximum.
So $E[S_T] = E[M]$, the mean of the bars.
The bars average 2.084.

feedback.correct: $E[M] = 2.084$. The rule is not a stopping time, so optional stopping does not apply.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. $S_T$ equals the maximum, so average the bars.

byKey.zero: You applied optional stopping. It needs a stopping time, and the step of the highest point is known only after step 10. That is look-ahead.
byKey.abs: You gave $E|S_{10}|$, the typical size of the final value. The maximum is a different quantity.
byKey.ten: You gave the largest possible maximum. It has chance $\tfrac1{1024}$.

explain.text: $S_T$ is the maximum $M$, and the bars give $E[M] = \tfrac{1067}{512} \approx 2.084$. Optional stopping needs $\{T = n\} \in \mathcal{F}_n$, and a highest point is known only afterwards. The reflection principle gives $P(M = m) = P(S_{10} = m) + P(S_{10} = m + 1)$.

screens.title: Stopping and looking ahead in code
screens.prose: Write `stopped_mean(N, rule, p)`. It enumerates all $2^N$ paths of a walk with up chance `p`. Each path stops at the first prefix where `rule` is `True`, or at $N$. Then write `max_mean(N)`, the mean of the maximum for the fair walk.
screens.question: Complete both functions.

widget.solution:
from fractions import Fraction
from itertools import product

def stopped_mean(N, rule, p=Fraction(1, 2)):
    """E[S_T] for a walk with up chance p. rule(prefix) is checked after each step
    and returns True to stop. T is capped at N."""
    p = Fraction(p)
    total = Fraction(0)
    for steps in product('HT', repeat=N):
        prob = Fraction(1)
        for c in steps:
            prob *= p if c == 'H' else 1 - p
        s = 0
        for k, c in enumerate(steps):
            s += 1 if c == 'H' else -1
            if rule(''.join(steps[:k + 1])):
                break
        total += s * prob
    return total

def max_mean(N):
    """E[max(S_0, ..., S_N)] for the fair walk, as a Fraction."""
    total = Fraction(0)
    for steps in product((1, -1), repeat=N):
        s = m = 0
        for x in steps:
            s += x
            m = max(m, s)
        total += m
    return total / 2 ** N
widget.prelude:
from fractions import Fraction
S = lambda w: w.count('H') - w.count('T')
hit2 = lambda w: S(w) == 2
hit1 = lambda w: S(w) == 1
five = lambda w: len(w) == 5
band = lambda w: S(w) in (1, -3)
widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests with exact fractions, each on at most $2^{10}$ paths. The rules `hit2`, `hit1`, `five` and `band` are defined for you, and `S(w)` is the position after the prefix `w`. At up chance 0.6 the mean is not 0.

hints.text: Loop over every path, adding steps and weighting by their chances.
Stop adding steps at the first prefix where `rule(prefix)` is true.
For `max_mean`, track the running maximum, starting from 0.

feedback.correct: All 10 tests pass. Fair stopping gives 0, a biased walk does not, and the maximum averages $\tfrac{1067}{512}$ at $N = 10$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the weight of each path and where you stop.

explain.text: `stopped_mean` gives 0 for every rule on the fair walk, as optional stopping says. On a biased walk the answer is $(2p - 1)\,E[T]$, which is not 0. `max_mean` shows what a look-ahead rule earns: a positive mean from a fair game.

screens.title: Stops, targets and the daily high
screens.prose: A fair strategy moves in £1,000 steps from £0. She stops at a loss of £3,000 or a gain of £1,000, whichever comes first. A second backtest sells each share at the best price over 4 days, counting the buying price. Daily steps are fair, £0.50.
screens.question: Fill in the three values.

rows: Profit per share the backtest reports (£)

hints.text: The first two use optional stopping with ends $-3$ and $+1$ from 0.
Stopped mean 0 gives $P \times 1 + (1 - P)(-3) = 0$. Then $E[T] = 3 \times 1$.
The third is $\tfrac{19}{16} \times 0.50$, since the best of the buying price and four closes has mean $\tfrac{19}{16}$ steps.

feedback.correct: A target chance of $\tfrac34$ after 3 trades on average, with no change to the mean. The best-price backtest reports £0.59 from a fair game.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the stopped mean 0 for the first two, and $\tfrac{19}{16}$ steps for the third.

byKey.r1c1: Use $E[T] = k(N - k)$ with distances 3 and 1: $3 \times 1 = 3$.
byKey.r2c1: You may have used the whole 4 steps, £2.00. The maximum of 4 steps has mean $\tfrac{19}{16}$ steps, so £0.59.

explain.text: Her expected P&L is $\tfrac34(1000) - \tfrac14(3000) = 0$: stops and targets reshape a fair strategy without changing its mean. Selling at the best price is not a stopping time. It reports $\tfrac{19}{16} \times 0.50 \approx$ £0.59 a share, which no live strategy can earn.

ideas: A stopping time decides from the past: $\{T = n\} \in \mathcal{F}_n$. The stopped process $M_{T \wedge n}$ is a martingale transform, so it is a martingale.
For bounded $T$, $E[M_T] = E[M_0]$. For unbounded $T$, monotone and dominated convergence extend it: $P(\text{hit } 10) = \tfrac3{10}$ and $E[T] = 21$ from 3.
It fails without a dominating variable: stop at $+1$ with no floor gives $E[S_T] = 1$. A highest-point rule is not a stopping time.

formula.name: Optional stopping
formula.note: Further reading: Williams, chapter 10 (stopping times and optional stopping); Shreve, Stochastic Calculus for Finance II, chapter 2.

summary.trap: A rule that looks ahead, such as the highest point, is not a stopping time. Fair-game results do not apply to it.

quiz.prose: A fair walk starts at 4 and stops at 0 or 12.
quiz.question: What is the chance it reaches 12?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The mean at the stop is 4, and $S_T$ is 12 or 0.

byKey.half: You assumed the ends are equally likely. The mean stays at 4, which is nearer 0.
byKey.ruin: You gave the chance of ruin. The chance of reaching 12 is the smaller one.
byKey.ten: You used an upper end of 10. The end is 12, so $12P = 4$.

explain.text: $E[S_T] = 4$ and $S_T$ is 12 with chance $P$, else 0. So $12P = 4$ and $P = \tfrac13$.

quiz.prose: The same walk from 4, stopped at 0 or 12.
quiz.question: What is the expected number of steps $E[T]$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $E[T] = E[S_T^2] - S_0^2$.

byKey.sum: You gave $E[S_T^2] = 144 \times \tfrac13 = 48$. The $S_0^2 = 16$ comes off it.
byKey.first: You may have used $4^2$. The duration is $k(N - k) = 4 \times 8$.
byKey.cap: You gave the upper end. The expected duration is $k(N - k)$, not an end.

explain.text: $E[S_T^2] = 144 \times \tfrac13 = 48$, and $E[S_T^2] - E[T] = S_0^2 = 16$. So $E[T] = 32$, which is $k(N - k)$.

quiz.prose: A trader watches a price for 20 days.
quiz.question: Which is not a stopping time?

options.text: The last day on which the price was at its starting level
The first day the price is 5 above its start
options.why: It is decided as it happens. You can see the day it first happens.

options.text: The smaller of day 8 and the first day of a loss
options.why: A minimum of stopping times is a stopping time. It is decided by the history to date.

feedback.correct: The last day at the start is known only at day 20.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the rule that needs later days to decide today.

explain.text: The first two rules are decided by the history to date. 'The last day' needs the future to know it was the last.

quiz.prose: Take the constant time $T = 5$ and a martingale $M$.
quiz.question: What does optional stopping say?

options.text: $E[M_5] = E[M_0]$: the fixed-time case of the theorem
Nothing: a constant is not a stopping time, so the theorem is silent
options.why: You thought a stopping time must be random. $\{T = 5\}$ is $\Omega$ at time 5 and empty before, which is in every $\mathcal{F}_n$ needed.

options.text: $E[M_5] = 5\,E[M_0]$, because the mean grows with time
options.why: You scaled by $T$. The mean of a martingale does not grow with time.

feedback.correct: A constant time is a stopping time, and the theorem reduces to $E[M_n] = E[M_0]$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check whether $\{T = n\} \in \mathcal{F}_n$.

explain.text: $\{T = 5\}$ is empty for $n \ne 5$ and $\Omega$ for $n = 5$, so it is in $\mathcal{F}_n$. The theorem then says a martingale keeps its mean, and $T = 0$ is trivial.
